title: Living, Dead & Never Alive
keyIdea: Everything belongs to one of three groups. Living things are alive now: they eat or drink, grow and have babies. Dead things were alive once, like a fallen leaf, a bone, or wood and wool that came from a tree or a sheep. Things that were never alive, like stones, metal, water and clouds, never ate or grew. Moving is not the same as living, and resting is not the same as dead.
familyTip: On a walk, collect a few things: a leaf, a twig, a pebble, a feather. At home, sort them into three piles: alive now, once alive and never alive. For each one ask, 'Did it ever eat, grow or have babies, or come from something that did?'

visual.caption: Was it ever alive? Drag each card into a box, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort things into alive now, once alive and never alive, trace wood and wool back home, watch a log rot, and check the signs of life.

kid: Things can be in three groups. Some are alive now, like a cat or a sunflower. Some were alive once, but are dead now, like a dry leaf. Some were never alive at all, like a stone.
Living things eat or drink. They grow. They can have babies. A stone never did any of these things, so it was never alive.

Some things are made from something that was alive. A wooden chair came from a tree. A wool hat came from a sheep. Paper came from trees too. So they were once alive. A metal spoon came from rocks, so it was never alive.

Be careful. A river and a cloud move, but they were never alive. A seed, a bare tree in winter and a sleeping hedgehog are still. But they are resting, not dead. Dead things that were once alive slowly rot. Stones never rot.
adult: Ages 6 to 7. This matches Year 2 Living things and their habitats in the National Curriculum in England (explore and compare the differences between things that are living, dead, and things that have never been alive). It builds on Living and not living and leads into habitats and how fossils form.

The three groups are about history, not appearance. Living things carry out life processes now; Year 2 children use eating or drinking, growing and reproducing as the test. Dead things carried out those processes once, including parts of organisms (bones, shells, feathers) and materials made from them (wood, paper, wool, cotton, leather). Never-alive things, such as rock, metal, glass, water and air, never did.

Common mistakes: thinking anything that moves is alive, so rivers, clouds, cars and fire count. Thinking anything still is dead, so seeds, bare winter trees and hibernating animals are called dead. Putting made objects such as a wooden chair or a wool jumper in 'never alive' because a person made them. And confusing 'dead' with 'never alive', so a stone is called dead.

In the lab your child sorts a cat, a stone, a dry leaf and a sunflower into three groups. They drag a chair, wool, paper and a metal spoon back to a tree, a sheep or rocks. They watch three months pass as a tree grows, a log rots and a stone stays the same. Then they sort resting things and parts of animals, and check the signs of life for a river, a cloud and a tadpole.

practice.prompt: A dry brown leaf has fallen off a tree. Which group is it in?
practice.hint: Was the leaf ever part of something living?
practice.explain: The leaf was part of a living tree, so it was alive once. Now it has fallen and dried, so it is dead.

choices: once alive, because wood comes from trees
never alive, because people made it
practice.explain: Wood comes from trees, and trees are alive. So a wooden chair was once alive, even though people made it.

practice.prompt: Mia finds {a} feathers and {b} pebbles. How many of her things were once alive?
practice.hint: Feathers come from birds. Pebbles are bits of rock.
practice.explain: The {a} feathers came off birds, so they were once alive. The {b} pebbles were never alive. So {a} things were once alive.

practice.prompt: In a box there are {a} dry leaves, {b} shells and {c} stones. How many things in the box were once alive?
practice.hint: Leaves came from plants and shells came from animals. Stones never lived.
practice.explain: Leaves and shells were once alive: {a} + {b} = {=a+b}. The {c} stones were never alive.

practice.prompt: A river moves and makes a noise. Is it alive?
practice.hint: Does a river eat, grow or have babies?
practice.explain: A river moves, but it does not eat, grow or have babies. Water was never alive.

pool.hint: Did a stone ever eat, grow or have babies?
pool.explain: A stone never ate, grew or had babies, so it was never alive. 'Dead' is only for things that were once alive.

pool.prompt: A tree has no leaves in winter. It is…
pool.hint: What happens to the tree in spring?
pool.explain: The tree is resting in winter. In spring it grows new leaves, so it is alive.

pool.prompt: A wool hat came from a sheep. It is…
pool.hint: Where does wool grow? Is that animal alive?
pool.explain: Wool grew on a living sheep, so the hat is made from something once alive.

pool.prompt: Which of these is alive now?
pool.explain: A seed is resting. Plant it and it grows, so it is alive. A bone was once alive. A spoon was never alive.

pool.prompt: Sam has {a} sticks and {b} metal keys. How many of his things were never alive?
pool.hint: Sticks come from trees. Metal comes from rocks.
pool.explain: The {b} metal keys were never alive. The {a} sticks came from a tree, so they were once alive.

pool.prompt: On a nature table there are {a} pine cones, {b} snail shells and {c} pebbles. How many things were never alive?
pool.hint: Pine cones came from trees. Shells were made by snails.
pool.explain: Pine cones and shells were once alive. Only the {c} pebbles were never alive.

pool.prompt: We leave a log and a stone outside for a long time. What happens?
choices: the log rots, the stone stays the same
the stone rots, the log stays the same
pool.explain: The log was once part of a tree, so it slowly rots. The stone was never alive and does not rot.

pool.prompt: A cloud moves across the sky. It is…
pool.hint: Moving is not enough. Does a cloud eat, grow or have babies?
pool.explain: A cloud is made of tiny drops of water. It moves, but it was never alive.
